children.text: tathā hi dūrād rūpaṃ paśyati akṣisthamañjanaṃ na paśyati ||
children.translated_text: Thus, one sees a form from afar, but does not see the collyrium located in the eye.

children.text: dūrācchabdaṃ śṛṇoti sati ca prāptaviṣayatve divyaṃ cakṣuḥśrotramiha manuṣyeṣu dhyāyināṃ nopajāyeta ghrāṇādivat ||
children.translated_text: One hears a sound from afar; and if their objects were only what is contacted, a divine eye and ear would not arise here among meditating people, just as the sense of smell and the others do not.

children.text: yadyaprāptaviṣayaṃ cakṣuḥ kasmānna sarvamaprāptaṃ paśyati dūraṃ tiraskṛtaṃ ca kathaṃ tāvadayaskānto na sarvamaprāptam ayaḥ karṣati prāptaviṣayatve'pi caitat samānam ||
children.translated_text: If the eye has a non-contacted object, why does it not see every non-contacted thing, both distant and concealed? For example, how is it that a magnet does not draw all non-contacted iron? And this point is the same even if its object is what is contacted.

children.text: kasmānna sarvaṃ prāptaṃ paśyatyañjanaṃ śalākāṃ vā ||
children.translated_text: Why does it not see everything that is contacted, such as collyrium or an applicator-stick?

children.text: yathā ca ghrāṇādīnāṃ hi prāpto viṣayo na tu sarvaḥ sahabhūgandhādyagrahaṇād evaṃ cakṣuṣo 'pyaprāptaḥ syāt na tu sarvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And just as, for the senses beginning with smell, the object is contacted but not every contacted thing is their object, since co-present odors and the like are not apprehended, so too for the eye the object may be non-contacted, but not every non-contacted thing.
But the mind, because it has no form, is simply unable to reach an object at all.

children.text: kecit punaḥ śrotraṃ prāptāprāptaviṣayaṃ manyante karṇābhyantare'pi śabdaśravaṇāt ||
children.translated_text: Others, however, hold that the sense of hearing has both contacted and non-contacted objects, because sound is heard even inside the ear.
But the remainder is what is called nose, tongue, and body.
